Educational References and Example Sources ⌄

The following references inform cooperative learning, differentiation, assessment, and classroom organization. They are not word-for-word sources for every example or step.

  1. Mashi bin Mohammed Al Shammari — 101 Active Learning Strategies (Arabic)Source for several strategy names and broad ideas; descriptions, examples, and diagrams were rewritten for this project.
  2. Cambridge International Education — Active learningAn overview of active learning and student participation in building knowledge.
  3. CAST — Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, version 3.0 (2024)Guidance on multiple means of engagement, representation, and expression to support learner variability.
  4. Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) — Collaborative learning approachesGuidance on cooperative learning, group roles, and peer interaction.
  5. Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) — Teacher Feedback to Improve Pupil Learning (2021)Formative assessment, feedback, and evidence of learning.
  6. Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) — Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning, 2nd ed. (2025)Planning learning, monitoring understanding, and reflecting after activities.
  7. Ministry of Education — Sultanate of Oman — Curriculum LibraryReference for grade and subject contexts; examples are illustrative and not attributed to specific textbook passages.

Research Sources for Individual Strategies

These references relate to the strategies in the guide and describe their research or procedural foundations. They do not necessarily support each illustrative example or suggested duration.

  1. Argument-Driven Inquiry — Sampson, Grooms & Walker (2011), Science Education — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  2. Peer Instruction — Crouch & Mazur (2001), American Journal of Physics — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  3. Just-in-Time Teaching — Mohawk Valley Community College, Just-in-Time Teaching — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  4. Faded Worked Examples — Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  5. Spaced Retrieval Practice — Dunlosky et al. (2013), Psychological Science in the Public Interest — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  6. Contrasting Cases — Schwartz & Bransford (1998), Cognition and Instruction — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  7. Model-Based Inquiry — Schwarz et al. (2009), Journal of Research in Science Teaching — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  8. Prompted Self-Explanation — Chi et al. (1989), Cognitive Science — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  9. Plan–Monitor–Evaluate — EEF (2025), Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  10. Engineering Design Challenge — National Research Council (2012), Framework for K–12 Science Education — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  11. Predict–Observe–Explain — Predict–Observe–Explain in Science Education (2026), narrative review — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  12. Problem-Based Learning — Strobel & van Barneveld (2009), Interdisciplinary Journal of PBL — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  13. Team-Based Learning — Michaelsen & Sweet (2008), New Directions for Teaching and Learning — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  14. Question Formulation Technique — Right Question Institute, QFT protocol — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  15. Active Flipped Classroom — van Alten et al. (2019), Educational Research Review — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  16. Interleaved Practice — Rohrer & Taylor (2007), Instructional Science — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  17. Two-Stage Collaborative Testing — Gilley & Clarkston (2014), Journal of College Science Teaching — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  18. Structured Academic Controversy — Johnson & Johnson (1993), American Behavioral Scientist — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  19. Mastery Learning — EEF, Mastery Learning Toolkit — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  20. Knowledge Building Community — Scardamalia & Bereiter (2022), Cambridge Handbook of the Learning Sciences — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.
  21. Refutational Text Learning — Refutation Text Facilitates Learning (2022), Educational Psychology Review — Research referenceSpecialized research source for this strategy; the steps and examples in this guide are educational adaptations.

Documentation Note: Classroom examples, diagrams, suggested timings, and progressions are editorial work for this application. Links to Oman curricula provide context, not proof of textbook origin.

Installable App

Add Strategies to Your Device

Full installation requires the published HTTPS website (such as GitHub Pages), rather than a local HTML file. After the first online visit, strategy pages and the interactive book can work offline; download the PDF separately.

Updates and Offline Storage

Version 9.2

What’s New in Version 9.2?

The unreliable AI assistant was removed. Lesson planning works locally and offline while keeping strategies, tools, and visuals.

  • Language and educational review of illustrative examples, including inconsistent examples and terms.
  • Consistent turquoise-and-gold identity with visual representations of active learning.
  • Rotating featured strategies on the home page.
  • Teaching Toolkit: saved plans, favorites, backup, and restoration.
  • Flexible search and individual links and QR codes for each strategy.
  • Teaching readiness checklist and printable plans.
  • Organized updates and repairable offline storage without deleting teacher data.
  • Better keyboard support, focus indicators, and reduced motion.
  • Larger mobile text, more prominent search, and improved offline updates.

Clearing temporary app files does not delete saved plans or favorites, but reconnecting may be needed to download offline files again.

In Chrome or Edge Use the address-bar install icon or the browser menu. On Mac with Safari select File → Add to Dock if available.

If the install option is missing: Ensure you are viewing the published HTTPS website, not a downloaded local HTML file. On iPhone use Safari. If it still does not appear, refresh or reopen after all files are published in the repository root.
